Title: Learning the dangers of storm surges in virtual reality: coastal leaders' attitudes toward VR as a risk communication tool
Brief Abstract: Educating coastal residents on the dangers of storm surge is one of the core missions of coastal community leaders. Virtual reality (VR) can help communicate risks by simulating storm surge events as if they are happening at the moment and allowing participants to virtually practice mitigation behaviors. However, VR must first be accepted and adopted by community leaders prior to implementation at large. Guided by the technology acceptance model, forty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with coastal community leaders after they experienced a VR education module of a hurricane-induced storm surge event. Themes pulled from the analysis revealed that attitudes and adoption potential of VR centered on perceptions of ease of use and usefulness. Media features that emerged as relevant in their decision-making process included VR hardware and content's emotional impact, novelty, ability to be distributed, and customizability.

Title: Weather Geeks Podcast Episode: Using Virtual Reality to Weather the Storm
Brief Abstract:
When a hurricane threatens, the most dangerous part often isn't the wind-it's the water. Storm surge can arrive fast, rise high, and turn familiar streets into life-threatening hazards. But what if you could experience that danger in a safe way, before it ever happens? Dr. Grace Ahn at the University of Georgia has developed Weather the Storm, a virtual reality experience that puts people inside a realistic hurricane scenario to show just how quickly conditions can turn deadly. By combining immersive visuals, sound, and storytelling, her work is helping coastal residents-and even emergency planners-understand the stakes and make better decisions when the next storm comes.

Title: Research and Development Portfolio Analysis: Lessons from Select Federal Agencies
Brief Abstract: This paper gives an overview of the inception, development, and maintenance of portfolio analysis management systems at three other Federal agencies: the National Science Foundation (NSF), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and the Department of Energy (DoE). The information in this document was gathered largely from interviews with agency staff, as well as from formal documentation. It also discusses how these systems have been used to inform and enhance agency operations. The best practices and lessons learned help devise a process for the development of a similar system at NOAA.

Title: The Changing Weather Information Landscape: Observations, Conjectures, and Thoughts about the Future
Brief Abstract: Numerous changes to information technology and media consumption over the last 2 decades have facilitated a fundamental shift in how people receive information, including weather forecasts. Historically, weather information was generally vetted through experts (often broadcast meteorologists) to members of the public in a relatively top-down system. Now, with the availability of internet websites, phone applications, and social media, people have an increasingly diverse set of sources from which to get weather forecasts. In this piece, we present results from CONUS-wide surveys that show this diversification of weather sources for nonroutine weather events. While older respondents still tend to get weather information from television, younger respondents are increasingly reliant on less traditional sources, including phone notifications, internet websites, social media, and family and friends. This shift to nontraditional sources means that a more diverse set of actors will have the opportunity to provide weather information to users, which could impact the quality, reliability, and accessibility of the weather information in the future.

Title: Examining Variations in Public Information Seeking for Severe Weather Events on National Weather Service Social Media Posts
Brief Abstract: This study examines the types of information the public seeks before severe weather events and how these preferences shift over time. Analyzing public questions posted on National Weather Service (NWS) social media accounts across 35 severe weather events between 2019 and 2021, questions were coded into eight categories: chance, location, timing, severity, impacts, protective actions, hazard, and miscellaneous. Location information was requested most frequently, followed by chance and timing. While demand for location details varied across county warning areas, it consistently ranked highest and increased sharply as events approached while interest in other categories declined. These findings highlight the importance of including clear, specific location cues (e.g., landmarks, major cities) in NWS graphics and posts to improve risk communication.

Title: The Color of Weather: Examining Associations for Color in Forecast Graphics
Brief Abstract: People associate colors with many phenomena and use those associations when paying attention to or recalling images in their minds. In this study, the authors extend color association research to weather phenomena, assessing implicit associations for 14 different weather hazards via a nationally representative survey of the U.S. public. Additionally, the study experimentally tests the importance of these associations, comparing the use of associated versus non-associated colors in a forecast map for cold temperatures and evaluating subsequent effects on cognitive processes like comprehension, recall, and risk perception.

Title: Flooding and Society Survey (FL24) / Introducing the Flooding and Society Survey Dataset
Brief Abstract: This dataset contains data from the Flooding and Society Survey (FL24), an annual, open-access survey effort designed to establish a baseline on public perceptions, understanding, and responses to flooding hazards and related forecast/warning information. It builds on the broader Extreme Weather and Society Survey series but focuses specifically on flooding as a hazard. The survey collects responses on topics like flood risk awareness, information sources, trust in warnings, protective actions, equity considerations, and societal impacts. It is intended for researchers studying risk communication, public behavior during flood events, and improvements in flood messaging. The dataset includes raw survey responses (likely CSV/Excel formats), questionnaires, codebooks, methodology documentation, and possibly select derived analyses or figures. It is part of the Extreme Weather and Society Survey collection on Harvard Dataverse.

Title: Tropical Cyclone Survey 2024 (TCS24) / Extreme Weather and Society Survey: Tropical Cyclone Wave (TCS24)

It is an annual, nationally representative survey that captures public perceptions, understanding, information-seeking behaviors, trust in sources, protective decision-making, and responses to tropical cyclone (hurricane) forecasts, watches, warnings, and related messaging. Topics typically include risk perception for hurricane hazards (wind, storm surge, flooding, inland impacts), evacuation intentions, equity in warning communication, use of Spanish-language products (if applicable in waves), and priorities for improving forecast/warning information. It supports research on hurricane risk communication, public behavior during tropical events, and societal impacts of weather products from NOAA/NWS/NHC.

Title: Extreme Weather and Society Survey 2025 (WX25) / WX Survey 2025 Wave
Brief Abstract: This dataset comprises data from the 2025 wave of the Extreme Weather and Society Survey (WX25), a nationally representative, recurring public opinion survey on how people in the United States perceive, understand, seek, trust, and respond to forecasts, outlooks, watches, and warnings for extreme/hazardous weather events (including severe thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes/tropical cyclones, winter storms, flooding, heat, etc.). It builds on prior waves (e.g., WX19-WX24) to track trends in risk communication effectiveness, public protective behaviors, equity issues (e.g., language access, vulnerable populations), information sources (e.g., NWS, apps, social media), and priorities for improving weather products. The dataset typically includes: de-identified raw/weighted survey responses (CSV/Excel), full questionnaire/instrument, codebook with variable descriptions, methodology details (sampling, weighting), and possibly derived summary statistics or figures. It supports academic research on weather-society interactions, NOAA/NWS forecast improvement, and risk perception studies.
